analysis.one_liner: Creates a free FCC website tool that uses AI to rate whether a message is likely a scam.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors on November 21, 2024, and never received a hearing, committee action, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Federal Communications Commission to build and post, within a year, a free online tool that uses artificial intelligence to help people spot scams. Anyone could submit an email, text message, web address, or photo of a letter or flyer, and the tool would rate how likely it is to be a scam. The bill defined a scam as any scheme to trick someone into paying money, handing over personal information, or acting against their own interest.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who receive phishing emails, fraudulent text messages, fake websites, or mail scams and want a quick, free second opinion before responding or paying. Older adults and less tech-savvy users, who are the most common targets of phone, text, and mail fraud, would benefit most from a simple rating tool. The FCC would gain a direct, public-facing consumer resource beyond its complaint forms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers targeted by phone and online scams

how_it_helps.text: The FCC must provide, within one year, a website tool that accepts submissions in many formats — emails, text messages, web addresses, and scans or photos of physical mail — evaluates how likely each is to be a scam, and gives it a rating on a scale the FCC sets [S2].

The bill defines scams broadly, covering any communication that uses false or misleading information to try to get someone to pay money, give up personal information, or act against their own interest, so the tool would cover phishing, fake invoices, and fraudulent mail, not just robocalls [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the development and operation of the FCC tool. No industry is required to change its practices under the bill, and no fees or mandates are imposed; the main cost is the federal expense of building, staffing, and maintaining an AI service, plus the risk of incorrect ratings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers funding the FCC tool

drawbacks.text: An automated AI rating could mislead as well as inform: a tool that scores a scam message as low-risk could give a victim false confidence, and a tool that wrongly flags legitimate messages could cause confusion; the bill leaves the rating scale entirely to the FCC and sets no accuracy standard [S2].

Users would be submitting emails, texts, and personal mail to a federal website, raising privacy questions about what happens to those submissions; the bill text sets no rules on data retention or use [S2].

The FCC's core expertise is regulating communications networks, and much fraud is mail- and web-based where other agencies (such as the FTC) already operate; the bill creates a new federal AI tool without addressing whether it duplicates existing consumer resources [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real but modest: the bill builds an advisory website tool rather than banning scam calls or text messages, and it offers no enforcement, penalties, or funding beyond a general instruction to the FCC. A free second opinion on suspicious messages would help many people, but the outcome would depend heavily on the accuracy of the FCC's AI and on users understanding its limits. The taxpayer cost is likely small relative to consumer scam losses, but the bill was so thin — one page, no cosponsors, no accuracy or privacy rules — that its design left real questions an honest supporter would want answered.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended; there was no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsor ever joined.

narrative.text: Representative John Curtis, a Republican from Utah, introduced the SCAM Platform Act on November 21, 2024, in the final weeks of the 118th Congress [S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which has jurisdiction over the Federal Communications Commission [S4].
No cosponsors ever signed on to the bill [S3].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died there [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one fought this bill in the record; it simply expired with no cosponsors and no committee action. Consumers gained no new federal tool for spotting scams, and the status quo — in which individuals must judge suspicious messages on their own — continued unchanged. The concentrated interests that profit from fraudulent communications faced no new tool and no new rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one in particular; scam operations unchanged

for.name: Rep. John R. Curtis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 21, 2024, directing the FCC to build a public AI scam-identification tool.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the FCC; chaired by a Republican in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 21, 2024, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, so there is no record of where the parties stood beyond a single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Fraud operations (phishing schemes, robocall and text scams, fake-invoice and mail fraud)
industries.note: A government tool that flags likely scams would make it harder for fraudsters to reach victims, cutting into the money they extract from consumers — losses measured in billions of dollars a year. The bill imposes no rules or penalties on them, but it directly threatens their revenue stream. It never advanced, so they faced nothing.

The bill does not require carriers or platforms to screen, block, or report anything, so it adds no obligations. A widely used government scam-rating tool could, over time, raise customer expectations that providers filter more fraudulent traffic, a mild indirect pressure.
